fn.en: Talk about experiences and finished past events, and know which one to use.

He was adopted by a family in Australia

Have you ever been back there

sub.en: Look at each pair. Does the sentence name a finished time, or does it run up to now?

items.q: I ___ in this city for ten years. (I still live here)
items.why: The choice turns on one thing: does the sentence name a FINISHED time? If yes → Past Simple. If not → present perfect.

items.q: I ___ in Taraz in 2010. (a finished year)
___ you go to Australia last year?
He ___ his mother again after twenty-five years.
He ___ her using Google Earth, in 2011.

items.why: RECYCLED: for + a length, since + a starting point.

items.q: I ___ him yesterday and we ___ for an hour.

rows: I’ve lived here for ten years.
Did you go to Australia last year?

You have been to Australia at some point in your life.

items.cue: Say it as an experience, with no time

items.from: We met in 2015 and we still know each other.

tts: I’ve just listened to a really interesting programme on the radio. — Yeah?
It was an interview with a man who lost his mother when he was a boy and has recently found her again after twenty-five years, using Google Earth. — Really? How did he do that?

Well, this man — his name’s Saroo Brierley — was from a small village in India. When he was only five years old, he was on a train with his older brother. He fell asleep and woke up fourteen hours later, alone, in Kolkata.
A family in Australia adopted him. Years later he started looking at satellite pictures for the station he remembered, and in 2011 he found the village.

items.q: Where did the speaker hear the story?
How long was the man separated from his mother?
How old was he when it happened?
What did he use to find the village?

acts.title: Two versions of the same family
text: My grandmother has told the story of 1962 about forty times and it has changed twice.

In the version I grew up with, her family left the village in the spring, travelled for nine days and settled in the north. In the version she tells now, they left in the autumn and it took three weeks. She is ninety-one and I do not think either of us knows which one is true.

What has not changed: her sister stayed behind. They did not see each other for thirty-one years. They wrote about four letters a year, which is not many, and in 1993 my grandmother got on a bus and went back.

I have known both of them my whole life and I have never heard either of them describe that meeting. My grandmother has told me about the bus in enormous detail. She has never told me what happened when she got off it.

items.s: The grandmother has told the story many times.
The two versions differ about the season and the length of the journey.
They did not see each other for thirty-one years.
She has described the meeting in detail.

write.q: Write six sentences about your own life and family. Three must use the present perfect (experience or a situation up to now) and three must use the Past Simple with a finished time. Include one “Have you ever…?” question.
write.model: I’ve lived in Almaty for six years and I still don’t know the north of the city. I moved here in 2019, in the middle of February, which I do not recommend. I’ve never been outside Central Asia, although I’ve wanted to since I was a child. My grandparents left their village in 1962 and settled in the north. I’ve known my closest friend since we were eleven. Have you ever gone back to a place you left as a child?

speak.q: Answer out loud: How long have you lived where you live? When did you move there? Have you ever been to another country? When did you go?
speak.model: I’ve lived here for six years. I moved in 2019. Yes, I’ve been to Turkey — I went in 2021, for two weeks in September.
